newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: IMF sees some inflation risk in Swiss policy.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees some inflation risk in Swiss policy.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said current monetary policy in Switzerland was not without risk for the long-term inflation outlook following a progressive easing since mid-1995.

"Looking ahead, the present stance of monetary policy is not without risks to the longer-run outlook for inflation," the IMF said in a report by a five-member delegation that reviewed the Swiss economy over the past week.
But the IMF said the recent reduction in the Swiss discount rate by half a point to 1.0 percent was "most welcome".

The IMF report noted that three-month Eurofranc rates had drifted up from lows around the time of the September 26 rate cut but said the weakening of the Swiss franc against the mark in the same period indicated that monetary conditions had not tightened and in all likelihood had eased further.
"The present constellation of exchange rates would not seem to pose an obstacle to a revival of growth, nor to be markedly inconsistent with fundamentals," it said.

The IMF said the present expansionary monetary stance should also help counter the dampening effect of long-term interest rates that were still high when measured by contemporaneous or projected inflation.
"The stance of monetary policy has eased progressively since about mid-1995, although, with the benefit of hindsight, too cautiously," the IMF said.

Referring to the longer-term risks of inflation, the IMF said the Swiss National Bank must carefully assess the unfolding situation to ensure that inflation remains low but also to avoid a premature tightening of monetary conditions.

"While the monetary base relative to its medium-term target path will provide a key benchmark, other indicators (e.g. broader monetary aggregates, real activity both here and abroad, financial market conditions and wage prospects) also bear close scrutiny," the IMF said.

It said these other indicators had gained importance owing to the impact on the Swiss economy of potentially volatile conditions in currency markets, especially changes in sentiment about Europe's single currency process.
